title: Efficient algorithms for Incremental Metric Bipartite Matching
claim: Our incremental matching method yields lower cost and far lower per-request time than the greedy baseline as the number of requests grows.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, ours vs greedy
description: Two side-by-side matplotlib line plots on MNIST data, both with the number of requests n (1000 to 10000) on the x-axis. The left plot, 'Average Cost vs. Number of Requests', shows average cost on the y-axis, ranging from about 38 to 50. The blue Batch Incremental PR curve rises slowly to about 43. The orange Greedy curve rises faster and ends near 49.6, so the gap widens as n grows. The right plot, 'Average Match Time per Request vs. Number of Requests', shows time in seconds. Greedy stays flat near 0.53 s. Batch Incremental PR stays near 0.00 s and rises slightly at n=10000. Each plot has a legend, grid lines and circle or square markers. The eye goes to the gap between the orange and blue curves.
caption: Plots of MNIST data
abstract: The minimum-cost bipartite matching between two sets of points $R$ and $S$ in a metric space has a wide range of applications in machine learning, computer vision, and logistics. For instance, it can be used to estimate the $1$-Wasserstein distance between continuous probability distributions and for efficiently matching requests to servers while minimizing cost. However, the computational cost of determining the minimum-cost matching for general metrics spaces, poses a significant challenge, particularly in dynamic settings where points arrive over time and each update requires re-executing the algorithm. In this paper, given a fixed set $S$, we describe a deterministic algorithm that maintains, after $i$ additions to $R$, an $O(1/\delta^{0.631})$-approximate minimum-cost matching of cardinality $i$ between sets $R$ and $S$ in any metric space, with an amortized insertion time of $\widetilde{O}(n^{1+\delta})$ for adding points in $R$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm for incremental minimum-cost matching that applies to arbitrary metric spaces. Interestingly, an important subroutine of our algorithm lends itself to efficient parallelization. We provide both a CPU implementation and a GPU implementation that leverages parallelism. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real world datasets showcase that our algorithm either matches or outperforms all benchmarks in terms of speed while significantly improving upon the accuracy.
